metadata.title: What Students Know and Can Do: Student Performance in Mathematics, Reading and Science – Volume I

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA 2012 mathematics volume reports results based on a sample of 15-year-old students drawn to represent the target population in participating countries and economies, using a booklet rotation design where each student completes a subset of items. The report describes how the mathematics scale is constructed from item difficulties and student proficiency estimates using a probabilistic scaling/modeling approach, and it discusses statistical significance and uncertainty bands for cross-country comparisons. The excerpt does not specify the exact sampling weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used in the reported estimates. Users should apply the standard PISA sampling weights and replicate weights from the PISA 2012 database when reproducing country/economy means, standard errors, and significance tests; if weights are not applied, uncertainty estimates and significance statements may not match the OECD results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an OECD results and framework description volume that reports scaled PISA mathematics outcomes (overall scale, process and content subscales, and proficiency levels) and explains how the assessment is designed and interpreted. The excerpt does not provide an explicit, reproducible analysis section detailing plausible value (PV) generation/combination rules or a missing-data strategy for an empirical model estimated in this text. Therefore, PV and missing-data handling are not reported at the level of methodological detail required for extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt describes PISA 2012 mathematics results for participating countries and economies, including both paper-based and an optional computer-based component (32 of 65 participating countries/economies). It explains that each student completed a subset of paper-based items (minimum 12 up to maximum 37) based on a booklet rotation design, and that each student completed a one-hour computer-based test in the computer-based survey for participating countries/economies. The report also notes that trend comparisons exclude countries where response-rate or comparability standards were not met (e.g., Austria 2009 boycott cases removed; Netherlands 2000 response-rate standards not met; UK 2000/2003 response-rate standards not met). No additional student-level inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., missing questionnaire items) are specified in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume explains the PISA 2012 mathematics assessment framework and how results are reported and interpreted. It describes the modelling cycle used in PISA mathematics (formulate, employ, interpret) and the content categories (quantity; uncertainty and data; change and relationships; space and shape), including how items are allocated to reporting categories based on dominant cognitive demand. The assessment uses a booklet rotation design: each student completes a subset of paper-based items (12–37) in two hours, and in countries/economies participating in the optional computer-based assessment, students complete a one-hour computer-based test. Mathematics proficiency is placed on a single continuous scale linked to the PISA 2003 metric (OECD mean 500, SD 100) and divided into six proficiency levels (Level 1 to Level 6). Country/economy comparisons are presented with statistical significance guidance and uncertainty due to sampling and limited item coverage, and trend analyses use annualised change with comparability constraints across PISA rounds.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is for an OECD PISA 2012 results/framework volume rather than an empirical ML paper with a documented predictive modelling pipeline. As a result, there is no student-level ML target variable, no reported ML algorithm comparison, and no explicit PV-combination or missing-data handling procedure in the provided excerpt. The main value of the text is assessment design, scaling, and interpretation of proficiency levels and subscales, so the ML-specific fields are intentionally empty.
